article: Does a spoon of cocoa have more magnesium than dark chocolate?
Compare the magnesium in cocoa by drink recipe and dark chocolate by the piece.
USDA SR Legacy unsweetened cocoa and dark chocolate, 70–85% cacao solids. Matched to example serving weights.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 5 g spoonful of the USDA unsweetened cocoa provides about 25 mg magnesium. A 20 g portion of its 70–85% dark chocolate reference supplies about 46 mg. The powder is more concentrated, but the chocolate serving in this example is four times its weight.
Work from the amount in the mug

For a two-mug recipe with 10 g cocoa, divide the powder’s 49.9 mg evenly if you pour equal amounts. Milk or a fortified drink would add a separate amount. Reading the number per 100 g as if it were per mug would give a much bigger estimate.
Use a matching label if your cocoa mix includes sugar or milk powder. This comparison uses plain cocoa as the ingredient, without anything stirred into it.

article: Does Parmesan add more calcium to dinner than mozzarella?
Compare a grated topping with a weighed portion of part-skim mozzarella.
USDA SR Legacy hard Parmesan and part-skim mozzarella. Sample serving weights.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: Hard Parmesan contains more calcium per gram in the USDA entries. But 12 g grated over pasta supplies about 142 mg, while 30 g part-skim mozzarella supplies about 235 mg. A comparison based on what goes on the plate reverses the ranking.
A little Parmesan is a different comparison

To work out the break-even topping, divide the mozzarella portion’s 234.6 mg by 11.84 mg per gram of Parmesan. About 19.8 g Parmesan equals that amount mathematically. The foods still differ in taste, salt and how they are used.
A freshly grated fluffy tablespoon can weigh differently from a spoon of finely packed cheese. Weigh the amount for a repeatable recipe.

article: Do dried figs or almonds add more calcium to a snack?
Put two 30 g portions on the same calcium basis and compare how a mixed handful adds up.
USDA SR Legacy dried uncooked figs and almonds. No added coating or mix-ins.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 30 g portion of dried figs contributes about 49 mg calcium in the USDA reference. The same weight of almonds contributes about 81 mg. Dried figs therefore supply calcium, but you need both the reference and the portion to compare them.
Add separate ingredients if you mix them

A 30 g snack split evenly between the two foods would supply around 65 mg. The calculation is 15 g of figs at 1.62 mg/g plus 15 g almonds at 2.69 mg/g. Both numbers describe total food calcium. They do not show how much would be absorbed by an individual.
The dried fig entry is for the dry fruit. Use a separate value if you buy fruit rehydrated or packed with another ingredient.

article: Which side adds more potassium, baked potato or butternut squash?
Compare two cooked side portions and see how a larger squash serving narrows the difference.
USDA SR Legacy baked potato with edible skin and baked butternut squash, both without salt.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: An example 150 g serving of baked potato with skin has about 803 mg potassium. A larger 200 g butternut squash side has about 568 mg. The extra squash narrows the gap, but it does not reverse it for these USDA entries.
Match the cooked part you eat

The squash contribution rises by 142 mg for each additional 50 g at its listed concentration. The figures use a baked preparation. Boiling in water, leaving part of a potato uneaten or weighing a squash with its peel changes which record or weight fits.
Use the edible weight after preparation. Butter or another topping belongs on its own line if you want a full dish estimate.

article: How much potassium does plain canned pumpkin add to oatmeal?
Add a measured portion of pumpkin purée to oats cooked in water and see which ingredient contributes more.
USDA SR Legacy canned pumpkin without salt and unfortified oats cooked in water without salt.
copy: A 60 g scoop of plain canned pumpkin adds about 124 mg potassium to 150 g oats cooked in water. The oats contribute about 105 mg before the pumpkin goes in. That gives about 229 mg for the two ingredients together.
Read the tin before using a pumpkin entry

The calculation uses a plain canned pumpkin reference. A premixed pie filling may include sweetener, other ingredients and a different number of grams per serving. Making oats with milk instead of water adds another ingredient, so the calculation would need a matching milk entry.
For two equal bowls, double both ingredients first and then divide the finished batch equally. That keeps the proportions the same.

article: How much folate is in a side of asparagus versus cooked beets?
Compare two familiar vegetable sides at the same cooked weight.
USDA SR Legacy boiled and drained asparagus and beets. Natural folate in micrograms.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: At 90 g cooked, asparagus contributes about 134 µg folate and beets about 72 µg in these USDA reference entries. Matching the cooked weight keeps serving size from deciding the answer.
Compare the side in the form you served

If a plate includes 45 g of each, the total is about 103 µg. That uses half the folate of each listed 90 g side. A salad made with raw shavings would need an entry that represents its uncooked ingredients. The table also excludes sauces and any other vegetables.
The values are total food folate. Use a separate label conversion if a fortified ingredient lists folic acid or dietary folate equivalents.
table: Natural folate at an equal cooked weight

article: Does edamame add more folate than avocado on toast?
Compare a weighed avocado spread with prepared edamame, leaving the bread out of both figures.
USDA SR Legacy raw avocado and prepared frozen edamame. Edamame edible beans and avocado flesh.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 50 g layer of avocado supplies about 41 µg folate. A 50 g portion of prepared edamame supplies about 156 µg in the USDA reference. The difference is in the two toppings, so it also applies when they sit on the same kind and weight of toast.
Keep the bread fixed when testing a topping

Some bread contains enriched flour and contributes its own folate. If you want the entire snack’s figure, add the same bread entry to both options. Edamame pods and avocado pits are discarded weights. The amounts here mean beans and flesh on the toast.
Prepared bean spread with water, oil or other ingredients would need its own recipe. The prepared soybean reference describes the beans.
table: Folate from 50 g of each topping

article: Can a small red cabbage side match cantaloupe for vitamin C?
Calculate the red cabbage portion that matches 150 g cantaloupe using USDA references.
USDA SR Legacy raw red cabbage and raw cantaloupe, edible portion.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 150 g bowl of raw cantaloupe gives about 55 mg vitamin C. About 97 g shredded raw red cabbage matches it at the USDA figures. The melon portion is heavier because it has less vitamin C per gram in these two entries.
Use the undressed vegetable weight

To do the comparison yourself, multiply 150 g by 0.367 mg vitamin C per gram of cantaloupe. Then divide by 0.57 mg per gram of cabbage. Those inputs describe two uncooked foods, and weighing the cabbage with dressing would throw off the calculation.
Ready-made slaw may include dressing, other vegetables and prepared cabbage with a different composition. This example isolates the cabbage.
table: Vitamin C in two close portions

article: How much vitamin C is in the little bit of jalapeño you put in salsa?
Scale the USDA raw jalapeño value to an 8 g ingredient and a shared batch.
USDA SR Legacy raw jalapeño. Amounts are hypothetical weighed edible portions.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: Raw jalapeño contains about 119 mg vitamin C per 100 g in the USDA entry. If you chop just 8 g into a salsa, the pepper itself contributes about 9.5 mg. The larger reference number describes far more pepper than this recipe uses.
Scale the ingredient before dividing a recipe

If four people each get an equal share of the salsa, your estimate is roughly 2.4 mg vitamin C from the jalapeño alone. Tomatoes, onions and citrus would contribute their own amounts. Use the weight that actually ends up in the salsa, especially if you trim and discard part of the pepper.
A pickled jar or a cooked salsa needs its own source. This reference describes raw pepper.
table: Vitamin C from the jalapeño alone

article: Can a bowl of bok choy add more calcium than a handful of watercress?
Compare a cooked vegetable side with a raw garnish and see what the portion does to the ranking.
USDA SR Legacy cooked drained pak-choi without salt and raw watercress.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: Raw watercress has 120 mg calcium per 100 g, compared with 93 mg in the cooked bok choy reference. A 30 g handful of watercress provides about 36 mg. A 150 g cooked bok choy side provides about 140 mg.
Compare a side with a garnish by the amounts served

The two foods have different jobs on the plate. The first comparison helps choose a reference food for a weighed sample. The second estimates how much the actual side contributes. At 75 g cooked bok choy, the calcium is about 70 mg.
Calcium content describes the food amount. The table does not calculate absorption. Keep the cooking state with your record when using these estimates.
table: Calcium from a garnish and a vegetable side
